s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: For a linear axis to successfully organize a composition of otherwise unrelated forms, what condition must it satisfy?
o: It must be an imaginary straight line with length and direction, requiring an anchoring element at each end to hold its visual force.
It must be a continuous plane or volume whose regularity gathers scattered elements into a single visual field.
It must balance smaller masses far from a center point against larger masses placed near that center.
It must be drawn only along the site's true north-south orientation regardless of the building's geometry.
n: Answer: B — Ching: an axis is an imaginary line of length and direction that requires terminating elements at both ends to anchor its visual force. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q1)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: A datum brings order to a disparate group of forms mainly because of what property?
o: Its regularity as a continuous line, plane, or volume that gathers and organizes an otherwise scattered set of elements.
Its function as an imaginary line of length and direction anchored by terminating elements.
Its ability to balance visual mass using lever-like principles around a virtual center.
Its placement at the exact geometric midpoint of a site.
n: Answer: A — Ching: a datum is a continuous line, plane, or volume whose regularity gathers and organizes a scattered set of forms. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q2)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Ching identifies three ways an architectural element can dominate a composition. Which option below is NOT one of them?
o: Giving it an unusually large size or mass.
Giving it a distinctive shape that contrasts with its surroundings.
Placing it at a strategically important location, such as a terminus or focal point.
Making sure it is entirely hidden from outside view.
n: Answer: D — Ching's three ways an element achieves hierarchical dominance are by size, shape, and strategic placement — concealment is the opposite of dominance. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q3)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Repetition alone is not the same as rhythm. What has to happen for repeated elements to actually produce a sense of rhythm?
o: The elements must be organized into a structured or alternating sequence that guides how the eye moves.
Exactly three identical components must repeat in a row.
Each repeated module must switch to a different material.
The elements must be laid out along a curving surface.
n: Answer: C — Simple repetition becomes rhythm only when the repeated elements form a structured or alternating sequence that guides the eye. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q4)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In architectural design vocabulary, what does the operation of 'transformation' aim to accomplish?
o: Change a basic form step-by-step through geometric adjustments, while its underlying grid and identity remain recognizable.
Disorient a viewer entering the building from outside relative to its interior layout.
Progressively alter a shape until none of its original structure can be identified.
Erase all trace of the original primitive volume through repeated subtraction.
n: Answer: B — Transformation is the incremental alteration of a form while its underlying grid/identity remains recognizable, per Ching's design vocabulary. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q5)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How can an asymmetrical composition still read as balanced and orderly?
o: It can't -- asymmetry inherently prevents true compositional balance.
By placing a lighter mass far from the center to counterweight a heavier mass positioned close to it.
By keeping every element the same visual weight regardless of distance from center.
By eliminating all but the single heaviest element near the center.
n: Answer: B — Asymmetrical balance works like a lever: a small mass far from the center can balance a large mass near it. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q6)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: When adding a modern wing to a historic masonry library, how does the transformation principle guide the architect?
o: By requiring the new wing to be an unaltered replica of the historic structure.
By having the architect study the old building's structural grid, rhythm, and proportions, then extending those same rules into the new design.
By demolishing the old library and rebuilding the whole thing in mirrored glass.
By ignoring the old structure's proportions entirely in favor of a contrasting new grid.
n: Answer: A — In adaptive reuse, architects study the historic grid, rhythm, and proportion of the old structure and extend those same rules into the new design. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q7)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which example below illustrates radial symmetry?
o: A skyscraper that twists 90 degrees as it rises.
A cluster of huts scattered informally along a river.
A round central altar surrounded by identical stone piers and seating radiating outward from it.
A long hospital corridor with matching rooms on either side.
n: Answer: A — Radial symmetry is a central element with identical parts repeating outward around it, as in a circular altar with radiating piers. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q8)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the key distinction between 'proportion' and 'scale' in design?
o: Proportion concerns the relationships among an object's parts and its whole; scale concerns how its size compares to some external reference.
Scale is set by engineers, proportion by clients.
Proportion compares size to the human body, while scale compares parts to each other.
Proportion is expressed only in metric units and scale only in imperial units.
n: Answer: C — Proportion is the relationship of parts to each other and the whole; scale compares an object's size to an external reference, usually the human body. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q9)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In the Classical Orders, what unit serves as the module from which column heights, entablatures, and spacing are all derived?
o: The diameter at the base of the column shaft.
The length of a Royal Egyptian cubit rod.
The total height of the building's main entrance.
Whatever dimension the head mason happened to choose that day.
n: Answer: C — In the Classical Orders, the module is the base diameter of the column shaft, from which all other dimensions are derived. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q10)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why did Renaissance architects such as Palladio base building proportions on musical harmonic ratios?
o: They held that the same ratios underlying musical harmony reflected a divine, cosmic order that architecture should express.
They wanted to confuse rival builders who had no musical training.
They believed hollow walls were needed to amplify indoor orchestras.
They thought irrational ratios were easier for masons to measure on site.
n: Answer: C — Renaissance theorists like Palladio believed musical harmonic ratios reflected a divine, cosmic order and translated those ratios directly into building proportions. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q11)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What does 'anthropometry' measure when used as a proportioning system in design?
o: The physical dimensions, reach, and clearance needs of the human body.
Seasonal humidity changes inside concrete rooms.
How historic monuments weather over time.
Wind-shear loads on tall building facades.
n: Answer: B — Anthropometry is the study of human body dimensions, reach, and clearance requirements used to size architectural elements. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q12)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: The Fibonacci sequence (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21...) closely approximates which proportioning system used in architecture?
o: The fixed Inaka-ma column grid.
The Golden Section.
The anthropometric clearance matrix.
The Tuscan order.
n: Answer: B — The Fibonacci sequence approximates the Golden Ratio, the basis of the Golden Section proportioning system. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q13)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What name did Le Corbusier give to his universal scale combining the Golden Ratio with human body proportions?
o: The Anthropometric Matrix.
The Modulor.
The Golden Section.
The Ken.
n: Answer: B — Le Corbusier's Modulor combined the Golden Ratio with human body proportions into a universal scale. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q14)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which of Vitruvius's three qualities refers to a building's usefulness and the efficient arrangement of its functional program?
o: Utilitas.
Venustas.
Commoditas.
Firmitas.
n: Answer: C — In the Vitruvian triad, Utilitas refers to function/utility, Firmitas to structure, and Venustas to beauty. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q15)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What do we call the spatial relationship where a larger volume completely encloses and contains a smaller one within it?
o: Adjacent spaces.
Space within a space.
Interlocking spaces.
Spaces linked by a common space.
n: Answer: A — 'Space within a space' occurs when a larger volume fully contains and encloses a smaller one. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q16)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which spatial organization type extends linear arms outward from one dominant central space, similar to spokes on a wheel?
o: Grid organization.
Cluster organization.
Centralized organization.
Radial organization.
n: Answer: B — Radial organization extends linear arms outward from a dominant central space, like spokes on a wheel. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q17)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which spatial organizing strategy uses a repeating three-dimensional matrix of bays to regulate a project's form and layout?
o: Linear organization.
Centralized organization.
Clustered organization.
Grid organization.
n: Answer: C — Grid organization uses a repeating three-dimensional matrix of bays to regulate form and layout. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q18)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Edward T. Hall coined what term for the study of the culturally shaped distances people keep from one another?
o: Proxemics.
Anthropometrics.
Ergonomics.
Kinesics.
n: Answer: C — Edward T. Hall coined 'proxemics' for the study of culturally determined personal spatial distances. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q19)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which of Hall's proxemic zones, roughly 1.5 to 4 feet, is generally reserved for close friends and family?
o: Public distance.
Intimate distance.
Social distance.
Personal distance.
n: Answer: B — Hall's Personal Distance zone (about 1.5–4 ft) is reserved for close friends and family. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q20)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What Japanese modular unit governs both the structural column spacing and the sizing of tatami floor mats?
o: Ken.
Shaku.
Tokonoma.
Tatami.
n: Answer: B — The Ken is a Japanese modular unit that governs both the structural column grid and standard tatami mat sizes. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q21)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term describes a beam or slab that projects horizontally beyond its supporting column, held up by internal tension and counterbalance rather than a support at its far end?
o: Portal frame.
Truss.
Tie-rod.
Cantilever.
n: Answer: B — A cantilever is a horizontal member that projects beyond its support, held by internal tension/counterbalance rather than an end support. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q22)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term names the design principle achieved when every visual and physical element in a composition is harmonized so nothing distracts from the overall concept?
o: Emphasis.
Contrast and variety.
Unity.
Contrast.
n: Answer: C — Unity is achieved when all compositional elements are harmonized around one overarching concept, with nothing distracting from it. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q23)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What kind of rhythm results when an element's size, color, or shape changes gradually and predictably from one repetition to the next?
o: Static rhythm.
Alternating rhythm.
Monotonous rhythm.
Progressive rhythm.
n: Answer: B — Progressive rhythm is created by a step-by-step, predictable change in an element's size, shape, or spacing. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q24)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which type of scale deliberately dwarfs the individual visitor to project the power of a state, religion, or institution?
o: Intimate scale.
Human scale.
Anthropometric scale.
Monumental scale.
n: Answer: C — Monumental scale intentionally overwhelms the individual to project institutional, state, or religious power. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q25)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which primary design element marks a position in space, has no length, width, or depth, and generates all other architectural forms?
o: Line.
Point.
Plane.
Volume.
n: Answer: C — A point marks a position in space with no dimension, and is the primitive generator of line, plane, and volume. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q26)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term describes how stable or concentrated a form appears, based on its shape, orientation, and relation to the ground plane?
o: Surface articulation.
Visual scale.
Volumetric proportion.
Visual inertia.
n: Answer: B — Visual inertia describes a form's degree of stability/concentration, based on its shape, orientation, and relation to the ground. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q27)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: When a basic geometric solid loses part of its volume yet still reads as recognizably related to its original form, what transformation type is this?
o: Parametric transformation.
Additive transformation.
Dimensional transformation.
Subtractive transformation.
n: Answer: C — Removing volume from a primary solid while its overall identity remains recognizable is a subtractive transformation. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q28)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What spatial effect does raising a base plane above the surrounding ground typically create?
o: A hidden, introverted pocket of space.
Complete continuity with no visual separation from the ground.
A weak, structurally unstable zone.
A clear sense of prominence, detachment, and territorial domain.
n: Answer: B — An elevated plane visually and psychologically separates itself, creating a sense of prominence, detachment, and territory. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q29)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Conversely, what spatial quality does a depressed base plane create relative to the surrounding grade?
o: It reads as a monumental marker visible from far away.
It maximizes structural tension across the site.
It forms an introverted, sheltered field of space distinct from its surroundings.
It eliminates all social activity around it.
n: Answer: D — A depressed plane forms an introverted, sheltered field of space distinct from — but continuous with — the surrounding ground. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q30)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term names the characteristic outline or contour that allows us to recognize and distinguish one three-dimensional form from another?
o: Shape.
Texture.
Position.
Size.
n: Answer: C — Shape is the characteristic outline/contour that lets us identify and distinguish a form. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q31)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Rotating a triangular shape around its vertical apex axis sweeps out which three-dimensional primitive?
o: Cone.
Pyramid.
Sphere.
Cylinder.
n: Answer: B — Rotating a triangle about its vertical apex axis sweeps out a cone. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q32)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term, often translated as 'spirit of the place,' describes a location's unique visual and emotional character rooted in its geography, history, and built form?
o: Parti pris.
Zeitgeist.
Partis.
Genius loci.
n: Answer: D — 'Genius loci,' Latin for 'spirit of place,' describes the unique character rooted in a site's geography, history, and form. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q33)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How does a highly polished, reflective lobby floor typically alter a viewer's sense of the space?
o: It mirrors the ceiling plane, creating an illusion of greater vertical height than the room actually has.
It makes the space feel dark and cramped.
It clarifies the room's geometric contours for the eye.
It visually lightens heavy columns by absorbing surrounding light.
n: Answer: D — A polished reflective floor mirrors the ceiling plane, creating an illusion of greater vertical height. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q34)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In color theory, adding grey to a pure hue produces what result?
o: A tone.
A shade.
A tint.
A new secondary color.
n: Answer: C — In color theory a tone is produced by adding grey (a mix of black and white) to a pure hue. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q35)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term describes a hue mixed with black to darken it and lower its value?
o: Tone.
Intensity.
Tint.
Shade.
n: Answer: C — A shade is a hue mixed with black, which lowers its value and darkens it. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q36)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which color quality has been shown to lower blood pressure and slow respiration, making it useful in calm healthcare recovery settings?
o: High-value red.
Low-value yellow.
Low-chroma blue.
High-saturation orange.
n: Answer: B — Low-chroma/desaturated blue is documented to calm the nervous system, lowering blood pressure and respiration — useful in healing environments. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q37)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In a split-complementary scheme built around yellow, which two hues balance the composition?
o: Green and orange.
Red and blue.
Red-violet and blue-violet.
Violet and blue-violet.
n: Answer: B — Yellow's complement is violet; a split-complementary scheme pairs yellow with the two hues flanking violet — red-violet and blue-violet. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q38)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What type of color harmony pairs two hues sitting directly opposite each other on a 12-part color wheel?
o: Triadic harmony.
Analogous harmony.
Complementary harmony.
Monochromatic harmony.
n: Answer: C — Complementary harmony pairs hues directly opposite each other on the color wheel. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q39)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In commercial kitchen planning, what name is given to the efficient layout path linking the sink, refrigerator, and cooking range?
o: The work triangle.
The concentric ring.
The circulation spine.
The linear assembly.
n: Answer: B — The Work Triangle links the sink, refrigerator, and range/stove for efficient kitchen circulation. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q40)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What clearance is typically specified between facing rows of commercial kitchen equipment so two cooks can pass back-to-back with oven doors open?
n: Answer: C — Commercial kitchen guidelines call for roughly 1500 mm between facing equipment rows when staff must pass back-to-back with oven doors open. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q41)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the typical minimum width for a secondary residential corridor so two adults can pass each other without turning sideways?
n: Answer: B — Building/space-planning standards set about 1200 mm as the minimum secondary corridor width for two people to pass comfortably. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q42)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How do 'personal space' and 'territoriality' fundamentally differ in environmental psychology?
o: Personal space is a portable psychological bubble that travels with a person, while territoriality is a fixed area someone claims and defends.
Personal space requires legal ownership papers; territoriality does not.
Personal space applies only indoors, while territoriality applies only outdoors.
Personal space is a fixed geographic zone, while territoriality moves with the individual.
n: Answer: D — Personal space is a portable psychological 'bubble' that travels with a person, while territoriality is a fixed area someone claims and defends. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q43)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which of Alan Westin's four privacy states describes being present in a public crowd yet unidentified and unobserved?
o: Reserve.
Intimacy.
Anonymity.
Solitude.
n: Answer: C — Alan Westin's 'anonymity' describes being unidentified and unobserved while present in a public crowd. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q44)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Under accessibility codes such as BP 344, why are doors and wayfinding signs required to contrast sharply with adjacent wall colors?
o: So low-vision individuals can more easily find paths of travel and emergency exits.
To match the minimalist look of the International Style.
To cut the cost of interior graphic branding.
To absorb noise reflections along evacuation routes.
n: Answer: D — High-contrast signage/door colors under codes like BP 344 help low-vision users identify paths of travel and exits. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q45)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How can color choice in a workspace help manage thermal comfort and energy use in a hot climate?
o: Color has no effect on perceived room temperature.
Cool colors can lower the perceived temperature of a space in hot tropical settings.
High-gloss neon paint physically traps cool air against the wall.
Bright pink paint blocks HVAC drafts.
n: Answer: B — Cool colors (blues/greens) can lower a room's perceived temperature, helping thermal comfort in hot climates. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q46)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In a fast-casual restaurant aiming for quick turnover, what color strategy should dominate the dining area?
o: Low-saturation, low-chroma colors that quietly calm diners for long stays.
High-saturation colors that stimulate appetite while producing mild restlessness that discourages lingering.
Pastel lavenders and desaturated sky blues to spark hunger and unease.
Monochromatic blacks and charcoal grays to slow movement.
n: Answer: A — High-saturation warm colors stimulate appetite while producing mild restlessness, encouraging quick turnover in fast-casual dining. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q47)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What structural/burial shift marks the transition from Egypt's Old Kingdom to its New Kingdom regarding royal tombs?
o: A complete move away from stone toward timber post-and-lintel framing.
A shift from visible above-ground pyramids to hidden, rock-cut cliff tombs meant to deter raiders.
The adoption of Roman-style concrete vaulting in temple design.
A change from open limestone colonnades to brick ziggurat platforms.
n: Answer: D — Egyptian royal burials shifted from visible Old Kingdom pyramids to hidden, rock-cut New Kingdom tombs (Valley of the Kings) to deter raiders. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q48)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What technological breakthrough allowed Roman architecture to break free of the Greek trabeated system?
o: The shift from the semicircular arch and barrel vault to the pointed arch and ribbed vault.
The discovery of high-tensile structural steel alloys.
A shift from marble columns to lightweight bamboo framing.
The development of opus caementicium (Roman concrete) and the true arch.
n: Answer: B — Rome's development of opus caementicium (concrete) and the true arch freed architecture from the strictly post-and-lintel Greek trabeated system. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q49)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why is Joseph Paxton's 1851 Crystal Palace considered a watershed moment in architectural history?
o: It introduced the first public electric elevator.
It was the first public building since antiquity to use hand-carved marble orders.
It marked the end of urban planning regulation in Europe.
It demonstrated that a massive structure could be rapidly assembled from prefabricated, modular iron-and-glass components.
n: Answer: C — The Crystal Palace proved that a massive building could be rapidly assembled from prefabricated, modular iron-and-glass components. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q50)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Put these design movements in their correct chronological sequence.
o: Gothic -> Renaissance -> Baroque -> Art Nouveau -> Modernism.
Renaissance -> Gothic -> Baroque -> Modernism -> Art Nouveau.
Gothic -> Baroque -> Renaissance -> Art Nouveau -> Modernism.
Baroque -> Gothic -> Renaissance -> Modernism -> Art Nouveau.
n: Answer: B — The correct historical order is Gothic → Renaissance → Baroque → Art Nouveau → Modernism. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q51)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In 'The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered,' what element did Sullivan use to express a skyscraper's threefold division, echoing a classical column?
o: A decorative, non-structural steel curtain wall spanning every intermediate floor.
Structural buttresses that thin progressively as the building rises.
A clear base, shaft, and crowning cornice, mirroring a classical column.
An uninterrupted glass wall exposing the structural core and MEP systems.
n: Answer: B — Sullivan described the skyscraper's tripartite division — base, shaft, and cornice/top — echoing a classical column. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q52)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which structural element was essential to Le Corbusier's 'free plan' and 'free facade'?
o: Pilotis paired with an internal reinforced-concrete column grid and cantilevered floor slabs.
A central masonry core carrying all lateral and gravity loads.
Heavy timber post-and-beam joinery that removes the need for deep foundations.
Load-bearing reinforced-concrete perimeter walls.
n: Answer: B — Pilotis, an internal reinforced-concrete column grid, and cantilevered slabs free both the plan and facade from load-bearing walls. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q53)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How does Fallingwater embody Wright's concept of 'organic architecture'?
o: Through a perfectly circular plan avoiding all right angles.
By mimicking biological forms like skeletons and leaf veins in the structural frame.
Through concrete terraces blended into the site's topography, echoing the natural rock ledges above the waterfall.
By using only biodegradable materials so the building eventually decomposes.
n: Answer: C — Fallingwater's cantilevered concrete terraces echo the natural rock ledges of the site, embodying Wright's organic architecture. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q54)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What design move did Gropius use to give the Dessau Bauhaus workshop wing its weightless, transparent quality?
o: Thick load-bearing brick walls with small punched windows.
A structural system of tensile fabric membranes and steel cables.
An asymmetrical arrangement of heavy stone pilasters flanking the entrance.
A continuous glass curtain wall set free of the recessed structural grid.
n: Answer: A — Gropius wrapped the Dessau workshop wing in a continuous glass curtain wall set free of the recessed structural grid, expressing weightlessness. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q55)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How did Mies express the Seagram Building's internal steel frame on its exterior while still meeting fire codes?
o: By adding non-structural bronze I-beam mullions to suggest structural rhythm.
By designing structural glass fins that eliminated the need for mullions.
By casting the curtain wall entirely from raw board-formed concrete.
By leaving the real steel columns exposed on the exterior without fireproofing.
n: Answer: B — Fire codes required Mies to fireproof the Seagram Building's real steel frame, so he applied non-structural bronze I-beam mullions to express structural rhythm. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q56)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How did Aalto bring a humanistic, psychological sensibility to the Paimio Sanatorium's design?
o: By designing glare-free lighting, curved splash-less sinks, and soothing colors suited to bedridden tuberculosis patients.
By organizing the plan around a central panopticon for constant doctor surveillance.
By using monumental, symmetrical neoclassical facades to project civic authority.
By employing harsh, raw Brutalist concrete to suggest sterile cleanliness.
n: Answer: B — Aalto tailored Paimio Sanatorium's fixtures, sinks, and colors specifically to the psychological and physical needs of bedridden patients. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q57)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In which book did Venturi argue for embracing complexity, contradiction, and historical allusion over Modernist purism?
o: Towards a New Architecture.
Delirious New York.
Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture.
The Language of Post-Modern Architecture.
n: Answer: C — Venturi's 1966 book 'Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture' argued for embracing ambiguity over modernist purism. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q58)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the defining strategy of the Pompidou Center's High-Tech design?
o: Ornamental Art Nouveau steel filigree decorating the exterior escalators.
Concealing all structure and services behind a thick stone-clad envelope.
Exposing and color-coding the structural steel frame and MEP systems on the exterior facade.
Constructing the entire building underground beneath an open plaza.
n: Answer: B — The Pompidou Center exposes and color-codes its structural and MEP systems on the exterior, the hallmark of High-Tech design. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q59)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which project's fragmented, titanium-clad forms brought Deconstructivism to mainstream global attention?
o: Eisenman's Wexner Center for the Arts.
Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin.
Tschumi's Parc de la Villette.
Gehry's Guggenheim Museum Bilbao.
n: Answer: D — Gehry's titanium-clad, fragmented Guggenheim Bilbao brought Deconstructivism to mainstream global attention. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q60)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics

q: What is the main function of a breeze block screen wall in a tropical envelope?
o: To shade the wall while blocking any breeze from passing through.
To cut direct solar glare while still letting natural airflow pass through.
To increase heat gain while allowing air through.
To act as a load-bearing column system for tall towers.

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In solar geometry, what does 'azimuth' refer to?
o: The thickness of the ozone layer over a site.
The sun's horizontal angular position measured along the horizon.
The sun's vertical angle above the horizon.
The vertical distance of the sun above the horizon line.

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: To minimize heat transfer into a building, what U-value should exterior wall insulation have?
o: A low U-value, meaning high resistance to heat flow.
A U-value of exactly 1.0.
U-value doesn't affect tropical heat transfer.
A very high U-value.
n: Answer: B — Good insulation should have a low U-value, meaning high resistance to heat flow. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q117)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why should highly reflective exterior finishes be used cautiously in dense Philippine neighborhoods?
o: They absorb too much moisture during typhoons.
They absorb intense heat directly into adjacent structures.
They can reflect intense glare and heat onto neighboring buildings, creating thermal problems.
They attract insects during monsoon season.
n: Answer: C — Highly reflective finishes can bounce intense solar glare and heat onto neighboring buildings and streets. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q118)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What principle explains why air speeds up when forced through a narrowed opening in a building layout?
o: The Venturi effect.
The Doppler shift.
Archimedes' principle.
The stack effect.
n: Answer: B — The Venturi Effect explains why air speeds up when forced through a narrowed opening. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q119)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: To maximize indoor air velocity from cross-ventilation, how should the windward inlet be sized relative to the leeward outlet?
o: The outlet must face the floor plane directly.
An inlet larger than or equal to the outlet increases velocity.
An inlet smaller than or equal to the outlet creates a pressure differential that increases velocity.
Both openings must sit at the same height on the same wall.
n: Answer: A — Sizing the inlet smaller than the outlet creates a pressure differential (like a nozzle) that speeds up indoor air movement. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q120)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What passive ventilation mechanism relies on warm, buoyant air rising through high vents while pulling cooler air in through low inlets?
o: The stack effect.
The Venturi effect.
Archimedes' principle.
The Doppler shift.
n: Answer: A — The stack effect relies on warm, buoyant air rising and exiting high vents, drawing cooler air in through low openings. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q121)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Which window type opens to nearly 100% of its area for ventilation while its angled slats still shed rain?
o: Jalousie windows.
Hopper windows.
Casement windows.
Fixed glass curtain walls.
n: Answer: C — Jalousie windows open to nearly 100% of their area while their angled glass slats still shed rain. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q122)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What landscape feature placed upwind of a building's air inlet can lower incoming air temperature through evaporation?
o: Dense shrubs planted directly below the openings.
A lawn paired with an open water feature for evaporative cooling.
A hedge serving as a natural fence.
A large asphalt parking lot with no tree cover.
n: Answer: D — A water feature or lawn placed upwind of an inlet cools incoming air through evaporative cooling. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q123)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What passive benefit do wide, overhanging open-air verandas add to a tropical resort design?
o: They fully seal the core building from storm wind dynamics.
They serve as structural counterweights against seismic movement.
They extend the building's lifespan by preventing material decay.
They shade the perimeter walls from direct solar heat while sheltering them from rain.
n: Answer: B — Wide overhanging verandas shade a building's perimeter walls from direct sun while sheltering them from rain. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q124)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What glass technology can reduce a window's solar heat gain coefficient without relying on external shading?
o: High-transparency structural acoustic glass.
Clear 6mm single-pane float glass.
Low-emissivity, reflective double-glazed units.
Wire-reinforced clear fire-rated glass.
n: Answer: D — Low-Emissivity, reflective double-glazed units reduce a window's solar heat gain coefficient without needing external shading. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q125)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What material property keeps the traditional Bahay Kubo from storing heat?
o: Massive load-bearing coral stone blocks.
Lightweight, porous organic materials with low thermal mass.
Poured reinforced concrete clad in volcanic tuff panels.
Wood panels raised on stilts specifically to absorb heat.
n: Answer: B — The Bahay Kubo's light, porous natural materials (bamboo, nipa) have low thermal mass, so the structure doesn't store heat. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q126)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why is a traditional Bahay Kubo's floor raised off the ground on wooden stilts?
o: To create a defensive vantage point during tribal conflict.
To maximize the roof truss rigidity during typhoons.
To isolate the house entirely from cross-ventilation.
To protect occupants from floodwater and ground pests.
n: Answer: A — Elevating the Bahay Kubo on stilts protects occupants and the structure from floodwater and ground pests. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q127)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What construction feature of the Bahay na Bato blends the climate logic of the Bahay Kubo with heavy European stone building?
o: Removing all windows from the upper residential level.
A building envelope built entirely from imported sheet metal.
A heavy stone upper floor resting on a lightweight bamboo ground floor.
A heavy masonry ground floor topped by a timber upper residential story.
n: Answer: B — The Bahay na Bato pairs a heavy masonry ground floor with a lighter timber upper residential story. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q128)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What structural feature in a Bahay na Bato is a pierced wooden screen near the ceiling line that lets hot air move freely between rooms?
o: Calado.
Volada.
Ventanilla.
Zaguan.
n: Answer: A — The calado is a pierced wooden screen near the ceiling that lets hot air circulate freely between rooms. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q129)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the purpose of the ventanilla sliding panels found below the main windowsills in a Bahay na Bato?
o: To serve as escape hatches during structural collapse.
To admit low-level cross-ventilation across the floor where occupants sit.
To serve purely as a decorative element with no airflow function.
To let hot air circulate freely between rooms.
n: Answer: A — Ventanilla sliding panels beneath the windowsill admit low-level cross-ventilation across the floor where occupants sit. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q130)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What advantage did translucent Capiz shell panes offer over heavy glass in the windows of a Bahay na Bato?
o: They diffuse soft interior light while withstanding typhoon winds.
They are completely soundproof against street noise.
They act as a firewall against the spread of fire.
They actively lower the humidity of incoming air.
n: Answer: B — Capiz shell panes diffuse soft interior light while remaining durable enough to withstand typhoon winds. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q131)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: On a site map, what does it mean when contour lines are drawn very close together?
o: An underground utility pipeline.
A steep slope or cliff.
A high flood risk zone.
A perfectly flat open field.
n: Answer: B — Closely spaced contour lines indicate a steep slope or cliff. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q132)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What does soil bearing capacity tell an architect during site analysis?
o: The required depth of the building's foundation.
The percentage of organic compost in the dirt.
How much weight the soil can safely support before a foundation sinks.
How much water the soil can hold during a heavy storm.
n: Answer: D — Soil bearing capacity tells an architect how much load the ground can safely carry before a foundation sinks. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q133)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What does a 'cut and fill' grading strategy primarily aim to achieve?
o: Cutting down all trees and replacing them with gravel.
Balancing soil levels to prevent erosion or landslide.
Digging deep trenches to search for hidden artifacts.
Minimizing the cost of hauling soil away or importing new soil.
n: Answer: B — Cut-and-fill grading balances excavated and needed soil on site, minimizing the cost of hauling material away or importing it. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q134)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is a 'bioswale' in sustainable site planning?
o: A shallow, planted ditch designed to capture, slow, and filter stormwater runoff.
A mechanical pump used to clear sewage.
A surface trench drain that channels rainwater to prevent flooding.
A buried plastic tank for storing drinking water.
n: Answer: D — A bioswale is a shallow, planted depression designed to capture, slow, and filter stormwater runoff. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q135)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What design challenge does a 'high water table' create for an architect?
o: The building must be built from lightweight timber frames.
The air over the site stays completely dry year-round.
Shallow groundwater makes basements highly prone to flooding.
It makes excavation unnecessary.
n: Answer: B — A high water table means shallow groundwater, making basements especially prone to flooding and requiring waterproofing. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q136)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How does a 'vista' differ from a 'panorama' in site design?
o: A vista is a framed, directed view, while a panorama is a wide, open view in all directions.
There is no meaningful difference between the two terms.
A vista can only be seen at night; a panorama only by day.
A vista is a 360-degree unobstructed view, while a panorama is hidden.
n: Answer: B — A vista is a framed, directed view (often along an axis), while a panorama is a wide, open view in all directions. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q137)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why is it better to align outdoor parking rows north-to-south rather than east-to-west?
o: It fits more cars into the same lot layout.
It aligns cars with the Earth's magnetic field to prevent battery drain.
It's simply more economical and easier for drivers to park.
It limits how long parked cars sit exposed to the low, direct east/west sun, keeping them cooler.
n: Answer: A — Orienting parking rows North–South limits how long parked cars sit exposed to the low, direct East/West sun, keeping them cooler. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q138)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why do sustainable landscape designers usually prefer native plants over imported exotic species?
o: Native plants are completely immune to solar radiation.
Native plants grow faster than exotic plants.
Native plants typically need far less water, fertilizer, and maintenance.
Native plants always grow as tall as the building roofline.
n: Answer: A — Native plants are adapted to local conditions and typically need far less water, fertilizer, and maintenance than exotic species. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q139)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What site element best blocks loud highway traffic noise from reaching a nearby residential building?
o: A wide open lawn with no trees, paired with a plain concrete fence.
A thin chain-link fence.
A bright, reflective white exterior finish.
An earth berm combined with a thick layer of dense shrubs and trees.
n: Answer: C — An earth berm combined with dense shrubs and trees is an effective passive barrier against highway traffic noise. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q140)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In site analysis, how is a 'microclimate' defined?
o: The unique climate of a small site, shaped by its topography, trees, water features, and surrounding structures.
A localized area whose temperature, humidity, wind, or rainfall differs notably from the surrounding regional climate.
The climate of a whole region spanning tens to hundreds of kilometers.
A weather forecast that updates every five minutes.
n: Answer: A — A microclimate is a localized area whose temperature, humidity, wind, or rainfall differs notably from the surrounding regional climate. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q141)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the primary purpose of a 'site inventory' at a project's early stage?
o: To create a checklist of all existing physical features of the site.
To calculate the final rental price of the building spaces.
To review existing site elements purely to estimate their cost.
To order the final construction materials.
n: Answer: C — A site inventory catalogs all existing physical features of a site as a baseline before design begins. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q142)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: Why is stripping all mature trees from a sloped site hazardous to nearby development?
o: It damages soil quality, weakening bearing capacity, which can also lead to erosion and landslide.
Tree roots stabilize slope soil and absorb rainwater; removing them raises the risk of severe erosion and landslides in heavy storms.
It simply violates the local ecosystem's balance.
It causes the water table to drop too quickly.
n: Answer: B — Mature tree roots stabilize slope soil and absorb rainwater; removing them raises the risk of erosion and landslides. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q143)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In landscape design, what is an 'earth berm'?
o: A deep trench used to drain sewage.
A raised, intentionally shaped mound of soil.
A shallow basin built to collect rainwater.
A decorative stone fountain.
n: Answer: D — An earth berm is a raised, intentionally shaped mound of soil used for screening, shading, or noise control. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q144)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the main advantage of using deciduous trees for solar shading on a building's south facade?
o: They shade the facade heavily in summer, then drop their leaves in winter to let sunlight through when it's welcome.
They serve as food and shelter for wildlife, boosting biodiversity and controlling erosion.
They block 100% of wind year-round.
They act as windbreaks and privacy screens that also support local ecosystems and habitats.
n: Answer: D — Deciduous trees shade a south facade in summer heat and drop their leaves in winter, letting sunlight through when it's wanted. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q145)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term names a broad, paved public walkway along a waterfront, beach, or riverbank meant for leisurely strolling?
o: Cul-de-sac.
Esplanade.
Alleyway.
Pleached walkway.
n: Answer: B — An esplanade is a broad, paved public walkway along a waterfront meant for leisurely strolling. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q146)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What outdoor structure is an open timber framework of posts and cross-beams, often covered in climbing vines, used to frame a path or shaded seating area?
o: Vestibule.
Trellis.
Gazebo.
Pergola.
n: Answer: A — A pergola is an open timber framework of posts and cross-beams, often planted with vines, that frames a path or shaded seating area. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q147)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What landscape element is a dense, continuous row of shrubs or small trees forming a living wall to mark boundaries or block views?
o: Fence line.
Parterre.
Hedge.
Bushes.
n: Answer: B — A hedge is a dense, continuous planted row that forms a living wall marking boundaries or screening views. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q148)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How do 'hardscape' and 'softscape' differ in landscape architecture?
o: Hardscape handles water systems; softscape handles lighting.
Hardscape means living elements; softscape means non-living elements.
Hardscape is designed by architects only; softscape by civil engineers only.
Hardscape means non-living elements (paving, walls); softscape means living plant materials.
n: Answer: A — Hardscape refers to non-living built elements (paving, walls), while softscape refers to living plant materials. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q149)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What was the core layout of Ebenezer Howard's 1898 Garden City model?
o: A giant factory complex with housing built directly on its roofs.
Self-contained, walkable towns surrounded by a greenbelt.
An endless line of skyscrapers strung along a greenbelt.
A grid dedicated entirely to car traffic with no parks.
n: Answer: D — Howard's Garden City model proposed self-contained, walkable towns encircled by a protective greenbelt. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q150)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the main goal of Transit-Oriented Development (TOD)?
o: Scattering future development further from existing districts around transit.
Building massive highways to speed car travel across cities.
Clustering dense housing, offices, and shops within walking distance of transit hubs.
Moving all transit networks entirely underground.
n: Answer: B — Transit-Oriented Development clusters dense housing, offices, and retail within easy walking distance of transit hubs. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q151)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What does the term 'urban sprawl' describe?
o: The uncontrolled, uncoordinated outward growth of a city.
The vertical growth of a city through high-rise towers.
Planting forests inside a downtown commercial core.
Converting old factories into public libraries.
n: Answer: C — Urban sprawl describes the uncontrolled, low-density, outward expansion of a city. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q152)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What layout does the New Urbanism movement champion for modern neighborhoods?
o: Mega-blocks separated by twelve-lane highways.
Sprawling, car-dependent cul-de-sacs with large front lawns.
Walkable, human-scaled neighborhoods.
Relocating residential communities to high-altitude mountains.
n: Answer: B — New Urbanism promotes walkable, human-scaled neighborhoods in place of car-dependent sprawl. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q153)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How does the Concentric Zone Model (Burgess) describe a city's growth pattern?
o: Land use organized in pie-shaped sectors growing outward along transit corridors.
Growth around several independent focal points or specialized hubs.
Pie-shaped slices growing outward along major transit routes.
A series of target-like concentric rings radiating outward from a central business district.
n: Answer: B — The Concentric Zone Model (Burgess) describes a city as a series of rings expanding outward from a central business district. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q154)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How does the Sector Model (Hoyt) map out urban land use?
o: Growth around several independent focal points or specialized hubs.
Concentric rings radiating outward from a central business district.
Pie-shaped sectors or wedges growing outward along major transportation corridors.
A single ring of industrial zones encircling the historic core.
n: Answer: C — The Sector Model (Hoyt) describes land use radiating outward in pie-shaped wedges along transportation corridors. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q155)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What claim does the Multiple Nuclei Model make about modern metropolitan growth?
o: Pie-shaped slices growing outward along major transit routes.
Sectors radiating outward from a single center along corridors.
Concentric rings radiating outward from a single central business district.
Cities grow around several independent, specialized focal points rather than one center.
n: Answer: D — The Multiple Nuclei Model holds that cities grow around several independent, specialized focal points rather than one center. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q156)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What term describes wealthier residents moving into a lower-income neighborhood, raising property values/rents and often displacing the original community?
o: Forced removal of people from their homes due to war, violence, or disaster.
Planting trees along public highway medians.
The influx of wealthier residents into a lower-income neighborhood, driving up costs and displacing the original community.
Structural reinforcement of old bridges against earthquakes.
n: Answer: B — Gentrification is the influx of wealthier residents into a lower-income neighborhood, raising costs and often displacing the original community. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q157)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What defines a 'megacity'?
o: A continuous metropolitan area with a population exceeding 10 million.
A continuous metropolitan area with a population exceeding 100 thousand.
A continuous metropolitan area with a population exceeding 100 million.
A continuous metropolitan area with a population exceeding 1 million.
n: Answer: C — A megacity is a continuous metropolitan area with a population exceeding 10 million. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q158)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What role does a 'greenbelt' serve in metropolitan planning?
o: A lawn placed in front of corporate office buildings.
Green paint marking bicycle lanes on roads.
A protected ring of open space that contains urban sprawl and preserves natural habitat.
A method of piping recycled water to city parks.
n: Answer: D — A greenbelt is a protected ring of open land encircling a city to contain sprawl and preserve natural habitat. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q159)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What was a common criticism of mid-20th-century Urban Renewal programs built on total slum clearance?
o: Forced removal of people due to war, violence, or disaster.
They frequently demolished historic, low-income neighborhoods without providing proper replacement housing.
They spent too little money on decorative monuments.
They drove wealthier residents into lower-income neighborhoods.
n: Answer: B — Mid-century Urban Renewal was criticized for demolishing historic, low-income neighborhoods without providing adequate replacement housing. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q160)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is 'urban blight' or 'urban decay'?
o: A design trend favoring raw, unpolished concrete facades.
The functional deterioration, abandonment, and economic decline of inner-city buildings and infrastructure.
The demolition of historic neighborhoods without providing housing alternatives.
Converting abandoned urban sites into new parks, markets, and cultural hubs.
n: Answer: C — Urban blight/decay refers to the functional deterioration, abandonment, and economic decline of inner-city buildings and infrastructure. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q161)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How is residential density typically measured on an urban planning map?
o: The total weight of residential buildings divided by road length.
The number of dwelling units per unit of land area.
The number of windows per building facade.
The number of cars parked along a residential street.
n: Answer: B — Residential density is expressed as the number of dwelling units per unit of land area. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q162)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is a 'Planned Unit Development' (PUD)?
o: A mechanical engineering blueprint for municipal water treatment.
A standard housing community with identical setbacks on every lot.
A flexible master-planned category allowing mixed uses, diverse housing types, and unique setbacks on one large parcel, bypassing rigid zoning.
An urban park made entirely of identical playground units.
n: Answer: B — A Planned Unit Development is a flexible master-planned zoning category allowing mixed uses and housing types on one large parcel. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q163)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What is the fundamental difference between 'land use' and 'zoning'?
o: They are identical legal terms in planning documents.
Land use describes what's currently on the ground; zoning is the legal tool dictating what may be built there in the future.
Land use is handled by private developers; zoning only by structural engineers.
Land use applies to rural areas; zoning applies only to downtown blocks.
n: Answer: A — Land use describes what is actually on the ground now; zoning is the legal regulation controlling what may be built there. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q164)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In Kevin Lynch's Image of the City, what term names strategic focal points where major paths cross, such as a busy train station or public square?
o: Edges.
Districts.
Nodes.
Landmarks.
n: Answer: C — Kevin Lynch's 'nodes' are strategic, busy focal points, such as where major paths intersect. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q165)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: According to Lynch, what is an 'edge' in a person's mental map of a city?
o: A major highway pedestrians use to cross town.
A skyscraper visible from any point in the city.
A linear boundary acting as a barrier or break.
A neighborhood known for a unique architectural style.
n: Answer: B — Lynch defines an 'edge' as a linear boundary that acts as a barrier or break between districts. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q166)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: How does Lynch define a 'district' in urban mapping?
o: A sharp fence separating two private properties.
A linear boundary acting as a barrier or break.
A medium-to-large area with a distinct, shared character that a person can mentally enter.
A single prominent statue at a major intersection.
n: Answer: B — Lynch's 'district' is a medium-to-large area with a distinct, shared identity a person can mentally enter. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q167)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What does Jane Jacobs mean by 'eyes on the street' for neighborhood safety?
o: Police stations should be built on every residential block.
Cities should install CCTV cameras on every power pole.
Active windows and storefronts facing the sidewalk let residents naturally watch over the street.
Streets should stay empty of pedestrians at night.
n: Answer: A — Jane Jacobs's 'eyes on the street' means active windows and storefronts facing the sidewalk let residents naturally watch over it. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q168)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What was Daniel Burnham's core philosophy behind the City Beautiful movement?
o: Creating monumental civic centers, wide boulevards, and classical grandeur to inspire civic pride and order.
Letting cities grow organically with no central planning rules.
Replacing public parks with vehicle parking decks.
Moving all commercial shops underground to keep streets quiet.
n: Answer: A — Burnham's City Beautiful movement pursued monumental civic centers, wide boulevards, and classical grandeur to inspire civic order and pride. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q169)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What daily schedule does Carlos Moreno's '15-Minute City' concept aim to restructure urban life around?
o: Requiring citizens to spend 15 minutes daily planting trees.
Ensuring commuter trains arrive every 15 minutes.
Making daily necessities reachable within a 15-minute car drive.
Making daily necessities reachable within a 15-minute walk or bike ride from home.
n: Answer: C — Moreno's 15-Minute City aims to put daily necessities within a 15-minute walk or bike ride of home. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q170)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What does Patrick Geddes's rule 'survey before plan' require a planner to do?
o: Thoroughly study a site's geography, history, culture, and existing population before drafting any plan.
Calculate a project's total financial profit before buying the land.
Interview neighboring mayors to align zoning tax laws.
Pour road foundations before assigning building zone uses.
n: Answer: A — Geddes's 'survey before plan' calls for thoroughly studying a site's geography, history, culture, and people before laying out any plan. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q171)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: In Ebenezer Howard's 'Three Magnets' diagram, which magnet represented his ideal destination?
o: The Town, with high wages but severe pollution and overcrowding.
The Town-Country, combining the city's economic opportunity with the countryside's fresh air and open space.
The Country, with natural beauty but total economic isolation.
The Wilderness, with no human infrastructure at all.
n: Answer: B — Howard's ideal 'Town-Country' magnet combined the economic opportunity of the city with the open space and nature of the countryside. (Source: TAPP Pre-Board Exam Reviewer, Q172)

s: Design Theory, Architectural Principles, and Related Topics
q: What global threat are Floating City concepts like the UN-backed Oceanix project designed to protect coastal populations from?
o: Severe underground tectonic earthquake shaking.
Extreme volcanic ash fallout.
Rising sea levels and coastal storm flooding driven by climate change.
High-velocity tornado wind damage.

How easily zoning laws can be read by lawyers.
The number of historic books stored in a public library.
How easily a city's parts can be recognized and organized into a coherent mental map by its residents.

Concentric circular rings expanding outward from a central temple.
Massive, high-density stone cities hidden in mountain valleys.
Linear settlements along coastlines and riverbanks for transit, fishing, and trade.

A massive empire of millions ruled by one remote emperor.
A dense network of factory workers in stone barracks.
A temporary camp of 5 to 10 nomadic hunters moving daily.

Grouping scattered, independent native communities into centralized towns to ease religious conversion and tax collection.
Replacing timber buildings with lightweight bamboo structures.
Reducing the farmland available to each family.

The Gridiron Mandate.
The Laws of the Indies.

On floating river rafts behind the municipal courthouse.
Miles away in rural agricultural zones.

The engineering study of underground concrete foundations.
The historical analysis of ancient Roman masonry equations.
The comprehensive, multidisciplinary study of human settlements, their growth, scale, and structure.

Rococo.
